summary: The system uses AI-based image processing and deep learning techniques to detect ships in SAR images, including during nighttime and cloudy weather conditions. It integrates AIS data to identify vessels, compare reported positions with satellite detections, and track their movements. It also aims to identify unmatched SAR detections, analyze ship movement patterns, and flag unusual maritime activities for further investigation.
details:
Illegal fishing, smuggling and vessels that switch off their AIS transponders are hard to catch. Optical satellites cannot see at night or through cloud, but synthetic aperture radar (SAR) can. Our project detects ships in SAR satellite images and checks each one against AIS broadcasts. It flags vessels that do not add up.

The system works in stages. First, it detects ships in a SAR scene using a classic CFAR detector or a trained YOLO model. Second, it estimates each ship’s heading from its wake, because SAR shows position but not direction. Third, it matches detections to AIS messages in a time-aware way. The satellite pass and AIS reports rarely share a timestamp, so a Kalman filter projects each AIS track to the moment the image was taken. Finally, an anomaly scorer raises alerts for dark vessels (seen by radar but silent on AIS), vessels reporting a false course, and AIS-only reports with no ship in the image. The results appear in a web mission console with a tactical fusion map.

The benefit is a clear answer to the question “is every ship I can see also telling me where it is?” This supports fisheries enforcement, marine protected areas, and search and rescue. It works day and night and in any weather. The intended impact is to give coastal authorities and researchers an open, low-cost way to find vessels that are hiding.

We built the system in Python, using NumPy, pandas, SciPy, OpenCV, Matplotlib and Folium for processing and mapping, and Ultralytics YOLO for learned detection. A Tkinter desktop app and an HTML/JavaScript mission console make it usable without coding. We trained models in Kaggle and Colab notebooks on public SAR ship datasets (SSDD, SL-SSDD and SARscope). Our SAR data comes from Sentinel-1, accessed through NASA’s ASF DAAC.

The project is creative in combining three things that are usually separate: radar detection, wake-based heading, and time-aware AIS fusion. Heading from wakes lets us catch vessels that spoof their reported course, not just ones that go dark.

We considered accuracy, honesty and usability. So far we have measured the pipeline on 50 simulated scenes, where it found all ships and flagged 94% of spoofed-course vessels. We are clear that this is a best case, and we are validating on real Sentinel-1 scenes. We also considered that AIS coverage varies by region, and that wake visibility depends on sea state. All code, notebooks and a demo video are open in our GitHub repository.

Team: Alex J Mathew, Jerin Francis, and an NPOL (DRDO) apprentice.
